https://www.asahi.com/ajw/articles/16748.text: Skip to content Twitter Facebook 日本語 English HOME What’s New National Report Politics Business Asia & World China Korean Peninsula Around Asia World Sci & Tech Culture Style Food Movies Manga & Anime People Travel Sports Opinion Editorial Vox Populi Views Special The Asahi Shimbun Opinion Vox Populi article VOX POPULI: Hungarian state TV’s apology also a reminder for global media Vox Populi, Vox Dei is a daily column that runs on Page 1 of The Asahi Shimbun. July 23, 2026 at 12:56 JST Share Tweet list Print A TV turned to Hungary’s state news channel in Budapest on July 7 shows a message that begins with, “Public service media cannot lie. We apologize for doing this for many years nonetheless.” (Reuters) In what could have been right out of near-future science fiction, the screen of Hungary’s state-run TV news channel went black and kept displaying the following message for about four hours: “Public service media cannot lie. We apologize for doing this for many years nonetheless.” This happened earlier this month in Hungary, where the general election in April had resulted in the first change of government in 16 years. The winning opposition party, the Respect and Freedom Party (TISZA), had campaigned for the “restoration of freedom of the press.” Defeated Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who had been in power for 16 years and whose political ideology made him an ally of Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, was known as “Europe’s maverick.” And he complained to the effect that the Hungarian media worked on behalf of the opposition parties. Under the Orban administration, the council that oversaw Hungary’s public news broadcasting was restructured to boost the administration’s dominance. A businessman close to Orban was entrusted with the management of a conservative, pro-administration TV station. And a foundation for “enhancing national awareness” was created to acquire and control financially troubled media. Thus, many media outlets formed the administration’s propaganda machine. According to Yusuke Ishikawa, a co-author of “A Dangerous Confluence: The Intertwined Crisis of Disinformation and Democracies,” Hungary’s public broadcaster has undergone a management overhaul in keeping with the new administration’s policy. The oversight committee’s membership makeup has also been rectified, so that both the government and opposition interests are represented equally. It would be meaningless if these changes only result in creating a new propaganda machine for the new administration. However, Ishikawa said, “So far, the parties involved are proceeding with care.” We in Japan would be wrong to think that what has happened in Hungary is none of our concern. Media outlets must always do “the opposition’s work,” so that the TV screen will never go black. I firmly remind myself anew of this constantly repeated warning: “Journalism is printing something that someone does not want printed. Everything else is public relations.” — The Asahi Shimbun, July 23 * * * Vox Populi, Vox Dei is a popular daily column that takes up a wide range of topics, including culture, arts and social trends and developments. Written by veteran Asahi Shimbun writers, the column provides useful perspectives on and insights into contemporary Japan and its culture. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Nikita and Olga Belov have tried to claim asylum in Finland but have so far found their case rejected. Photograph: Nikita Belov View image in fullscreen Nikita and Olga Belov have tried to claim asylum in Finland but have so far found their case rejected. Photograph: Nikita Belov Finland Russian family denied asylum in Finland fear reprisals for pro-Ukraine activism Nikita and Olga Belov say they will be persecuted on return to Moscow but are yet to convince Finnish authorities Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent Sun 9 Aug 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 03.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Russian family faces deportation from Finland after repeatedly being denied asylum – despite the threat of arrest, imprisonment and potential torture for their pro-Ukrainian activism. Nikita and Olga Belov fled their homeland in 2022 after attracting the attention of Russian authorities – including military summons, threatening messages and attempts to locate them – after expressing opposition to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Nikita, 25, left his engineering job at a research institute in Moscow specialising in metallurgical technologies after finding out the work he was doing was connected to the Russian war effort. Since arriving in Finland on visas, Nikita and his mother, Olga, 55, a nurse anaesthetist, have been vocal supporters of Ukraine and public in their active support and coordination of aid sent to the country and its armed forces. But the Finnish immigration service told the mother and son that despite this they face “no real risk” if they return to Russia. In April, they were detained by Finnish authorities pending deportation. They were later released after a court intervention but are now awaiting a decision that could result in them being deported within weeks. View image in fullscreen Nikita Belov and his mother, Olga, are strong supporters of Ukraine and critics of Putin’s war. Photograph: Nikita Belov The Belov case is understood to be one of many of Russians being denied asylum in neighbouring Finland where legal experts deem their future risk and human rights have not been sufficiently assessed. Between February 2022 and June 2026, the Finnish immigration service deported 1,039 Russians according to official statistics: the most of any nationality. During the same period, 1,109 of 1,342 Russians were refused entry to Finland in connection with a negative asylum application. Since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Finland’s relationship with its neighbour has shifted drastically . Previously, Finland was a popular tourism destination for Russians and there were several well-used border crossings. It has since indefinitely closed its entire border, accusing Moscow of directing asylum seekers to Finland in a “hybrid operation”. Russia has also expanded its military bases on the border, while Nato – which Finland joined in 2023 – has conducted training exercises in the country. View image in fullscreen Nikita and Olga have been in Finland since 2022. Photograph: Nikita Belov Nikita said his problems in Russia started when he realised that his boss had lied when he had told him that the project he was working on was not linked to the war effort. When he tried to come off the project, he said his boss threatened him with arrest or being sent to the frontline. “After that I realised I cannot leave this job without consequences and that we had to think about the situation,” Nikita said. His mother, he said, was then called by the military to ask about him and their house was visited by police. They soon came to the conclusion that they had no option but to leave Russia. “Now we realise if we come back we will be arrested immediately and go to jail and be tortured,” Nikita said. In Finland they have volunteered at their local Ukraine centre and contributed to humanitarian support, including help for first aid, food, clothes, Starlink equipment and a 3D printer, for which they received a video thank you message from Ukrainian soldiers. “We try to adapt, try to support Ukraine, try to state our opinion, because it is very important to help Ukraine. Help them strike back,” he said. View image in fullscreen Nikita and Olga Belov continue to volunteer for pro-Ukraine causes. Photograph: Nikita Belov The mother and son first applied for asylum in Finland in 2022 but it was refused, after which they unsuccessfully appealed. This year they applied again and were refused and were sent a deportation order. They were then placed in a detention centre awaiting deportation but after a court intervention were allowed to go home before a final decision. “There were all bad things in our minds. It was like the start of torture because it was a totally traumatic experience,” Nikita said. “At the time we really tried to prepare for our death.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion Since then they have suffered with their mental health and undergone panic attacks as they wait for the decision of the court. Their lawyer, who requested not to be named for security reasons, said the Belovs are very likely to be at risk if they are deported to Russia. Nikita’s work history will also put them at risk, the lawyer said. In a previous role he said he had access to confidential government information. While it has long been difficult to get asylum in Finland, the lawyer said that recent changes on the border and to asylum procedure, including reduced access to legal aid, has made it even harder. “It’s even more difficult to get refugee status, even with clear political opinion showing. We really have to fight these cases to get the status that was earlier easier to get.” Blinded by War: documenting the aftermath of injury in Ukraine – photo essay Read more The political activist and Putin critic Bill Browder , who is the head of the Global Magnitsky Justice Campaign, said the case is “a defining test of Europe’s commitment to protecting those who have risked everything to oppose Putin’s war”. Browder, whose friend and lawyer Sergei Magnitsky died at the hands of Putin’s regime , added: “If people who refused to support aggression, openly opposed the regime, and now face persecution are denied protection, it could create a dangerous precedent that discourages others from taking a stand against authoritarianism.” A Finnish immigration service spokesperson said it could not comment on individual cases. Antti Lehtinen, the director of the department for international protection, which is part of the Finnish immigration service, added: “The situation of each applicant is assessed individually, taking into account their personal circumstances. “For example, opposition to the war in Ukraine and related activities may constitute grounds for persecution based on political opinion. If we assess that a person’s political opinion or activities place them at risk of persecution or serious harm in Russia, they will be granted international protection.” Explore more on these topics Finland Ukraine Russia Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://telex.hu/g7/penz/2026/08/12/alla.text: Menü Kereső Egyelőre csak szépségtapasz a magyar államadósságon a forint erősödése Pénz Fotó: Oláh Tibor / MTI Stubnya Bence Több mint 1500 milliárd forinttal csökkent a magyar állam devizaadóssága az év első felében a forint erősödésének köszönhetően. A teljes államadósság ugyanakkor összességében több mint 2500 milliárd forinttal emelkedett, és elérte a 63 082 milliárd forintot – írta a Népszava . A gyors növekedést két fő tényező magyarázza: a választás előtti költségvetési osztogatások forrásigénye, valamint hogy az Államadósság Kezelő Központ még a választások előtt biztosította az év második felére a kiadásokhoz és az államadósság törlesztéséhez szükséges forrásokat. Felülnézet : a devizaadósság átértékelődése jó hír ugyan, de az állam nagyrészt csak az adósság lejáratakor (esetleg előtörlesztésekor) jut majd hozzá az ebből keletkező nyereséghez. A Magyar Nemzeti Bank adatai szerint a tavaly december végi 74,6 százalékról június végéig 77,9 százalékra nőtt az adósság GDP-hez viszonyított szintje, és innen az év végéig 74,6 százalékra csökkenhet. Tágabb kontextus: a választások óta az állam olcsóbban tudja magát finanszírozni , ami miatt a lakossági állampapírok kamatait is többször csökkentették már. Ez ugyan javítja a büdzsé egyenlegét, de a kormányváltás óta az is kiderült, hogy az új kormány rosszabb költségvetési helyzetet örökölt , mint amiről az előző kormány kommunikációja alapján tudni lehetett. Júliusban viszont már harmadik hónapja volt többletes a költségvetés, a hétfőn közzétett legfrissebb adatok szerint az előző hónapban például 524,3 milliárd forinttal. Ahogy erre a Portfolio.hu cikke emlékeztetett, ekkora többletre 22 éve nem volt példa. Reakció : „a részletes adatokat még nem ismerjük, de a gyorstájékoztatóból kiolvasható, hogy a választások előtt a korábbi kormány »tövig nyomta a gázt«, és jelentős részben – minden bizonnyal – előrehozott kifizetéseket hajtott végre. Az utóbbi egy-két hónapban ennek a korrekcióját látjuk” – írta Trippon Mariann, a CIB Bank vezető elemzője a G7 megkeresésére. A Pénzügyminisztérium nyár eleji technikai kivetítése alapján az idei hiány 7,5 százalék lesz, az új 2026-os költségvetés augusztus végén-szeptember elején jön ki. A CIB Bank előrejelzése ennél valamivel alacsonyabb, minimálisan 7 százalék alatti hiánnyal kalkulál. Mi várható? Március eleje és június vége között a forint jelentősen erősödött az euróval szemben, a 355 körüli árfolyamról ugyanakkor azóta 360 fölé gyengült, a napokban 365 környékén járt, ami alapján már csak kisebb potenciál lehet a devizaadósság további átértékelődésében. A költségvetés szempontjából is nagy jelentősége lesz, hogyan alakul az év hátralevő részében az energiahelyzet. Ha az üzemanyagárak elszállása miatt a kormány beavatkozik, vagy ha a Duna vízszintje miatt tartósan csökken a paksi atomerőmű teljesítménye, az ronthatja a költségvetési egyenleget is. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Legfontosabb Friss hírek

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-attacks-wi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ItPp Experts say the attacks, including this strike on a Wildberries warehouse outside Moscow on July 18, are part of a strategy to 'bring the war home' to Russian civilians Image: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP Advertisement Early Sunday, a fire broke out in a warehouse belonging to Russia's largest online marketplace , Wildberries, in the town of Podolsk, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Moscow. The fire was the result of a large-scale overnight attack by Ukrainian drones , most of which were intercepted by Russian air defenses. On Friday, Ukraine struck a different Wildberries warehouse, in Tver, north of Moscow. The day before, it had set fire to another warehouse in Salavat, further east. About 20 Wildberries logistics hubs have been under near-daily attack in the past few weeks . At least nine employees have been confirmed dead, and scores injured, while a handful of the storehouses have halted operations. The Moscow-based e-commerce consultancy Data Insight estimates Wildberries has lost as much as 480 billion rubles worth of goods ($5.7 billion/€4.9 billion) and about a third of its warehouse space. Combined damaged to the company and its sellers are estimated as high as 800 billion rubles ($9.5 billion). Putin admits Ukraine's drones are hurting Russia's economy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video While Kyiv argues the retailer helps supply Russia's military , Moscow maintains it serves only civilian purposes. Either way, the attacks have been placing an increased strain on Russia's economy. "I think [Ukraine is] going after a choke point," Fabrice Pothier, CEO of the geopolitical consultancy firm Rasmussen Global, told DW. "Wildberries is, in a way, a choke point of Russian society and the Russian economy." Wildberries: Russia's Amazon Wildberries is often described as Russia's answer to the Amazon marketplace . Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the ensuing sanctions on Russian trade , many online e-commerce platforms such as Amazon withdrew from the region. In response, Russian authorities permitted so-called parallel imports, essentially allowing Russian companies to sidestep sanctions by importing goods without the consent of the original rights holders. These companies drastically undercut conventional prices, allowing their sales volume to skyrocket. In the case of Wildberries, for example, revenue increased sevenfold between 2021 and 2025. Its competitor, Ozon, offers similarly staggering numbers, with a reported $49.3 million revenue and 59% growth in 2025. Today, Wildberries is the largest e-commerce platform in the country, controlling about half of the respective market. Ozon dominates about 30% of the market. Together, they handle goods and services equivalent to about 8.5% of the Russia's gross domestic product (GDP). Why is Ukraine targeting warehouses? Following the initial attacks in mid-July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy argued that the warehouses struck were "elements of Russian logistics [...] used to distribute equipment for the war: navigation systems, components for drone production, and other supplies for the Russian army." The Kremlin has consistently rejected this claim. But an analysis by the independent outlet Verska identified "tens of thousands of military and dual-use goods" on the platform between May and August this year, amounting in sales worth hundred of millions of rubles. Why Ukraine is targeting Russia's biggest online retailer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Mykhailo Podolyak, adviser to the head of Zelenskyy's office, said interrupting the flow of military goods to the front lines was just one reason for attacking the company's storage space. Disrupting a business with around 6 trillion rubels in turnover, he told DW, would also affect its creditors, including Sverbank and VTB, both of which are majority state-owned. Not only could this drain state coffers, "if [the company] were to go bankrupt, it will probably have a domino-effect on the economy," as Pothier explained. And "there is a bigger objective at play," the consultant added, "which is to bring back war to its sender" by disrupting civilian life. As many as 400,000 sellers have been affected by the attacks, the Russian Association of Electronic Trading Platforms reported. As a result, civilians are losing sources of income, access to goods and services, and, increasingly, a sense of normality. Wildberries is Russia's largest e-commerce platform, a part of life for millions of people Image: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS The platform hosts over 1 million sellers — most of them small- and medium-sized — and reaches some 80 million users each month. But targeting Wildberries was also meant to send a message to Russian elites, according to Podolyak. These include the billionaire Suleiman Kerimov, the diplomat Anton Vaino or politician Alexey Gromov, all of whom are counted in Putin's inner circle, and possibly have varying degrees of involvement with the Wildberries company. What makes Wildberries a target? Wildberries has been investing in massive logistics hubs. The largest span the size of several dozen soccer fields, making them fairly easy — and highly flammable — targets. With hundreds of thousands of retailers affected in the attacks, Wildberries head and co-founder Tatyana Kim has now turned to the government for financial support Image: Evgeniy Razumniy/Kommersant Photo/Sipa USA/picture alliance The company is also said to have incurred substantial debt, with some questioning whether it is still able to service them. According to financial reporting of its main operating entity, RWB LLC, short-term borrowing spiked nearly eightfold between 2024 and 2025. Along with long-term liabilities, Wildberries' debt may be as high as $14 billion, with VTB as the single-largest creditor. Now, the other state-backed creditor, Sberbank, has signaled it is preparing to absorb losses. In response to attack on Wildberries' warehouses, Chief Financial Officer Taras Skvortsov said: "Regarding [Wildberries'] credit quality, there is indeed damage. [...] Their financial condition and potential future cash flow have decreased." Billionaire Tatyana Kim, CEO and co-founder of Wildberries, has now reportedly turned to the government for support. While the government has confirmed talks, no details on a potential decision have emerged. It is expected, however, that VTB will play a key role in rescue efforts. This article was originally written in Russian. It was updated on August 15 to reflect the latest developments. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Air support in fighting the fire in the High Fens nature reserve is crucial owing to the complex terrain where heavy vehicles risk sinking. Photograph: Nicolas Lambert/Belga/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Air support in fighting the fire in the High Fens nature reserve is crucial owing to the complex terrain where heavy vehicles risk sinking. Photograph: Nicolas Lambert/Belga/Shutterstock Wildfires Greek wildfire kills two people as aircraft deployed to blaze at Belgian nature reserve Couple die in Salamis and Belgium battling its biggest fire in more than a century near German border Angela Giuffrida and agencies Sun 16 Aug 2026 14.23 EDT First published on Sun 16 Aug 2026 11.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An elderly couple died in fires on the Greek island of Salamis on Sunday and a fire ravaged Belgium’s largest nature reserve, in the latest wave of European wildfires. The couple died outside their home in the Peristeria beach area of Salamis, Greece’s coastguard said. More than 500 people were ordered to evacuate. In Belgium, a wildfire that broke out on Friday in the High Fens, a large nature reserve popular with hikers, had ravaged about 3,000 hectares (7,400 acres) of land and was encroaching on the border with Germany by early Sunday morning. Map of Greek wildfire About 600 people in the municipalities of Waimes and Bütgenbach, in Liège province, were told on Saturday to evacuate from their homes, and tourists were also advised to leave, as winds shifted and smoke spread. Of those who followed the order, about 20 spent the night in a sports hall, while others sought refuge with family and friends. Hervé Jamar, the governor of Liège, said more than 250 firefighters and emergency staff were involved in the operation, including firefighters from Germany. View image in fullscreen Farmers have used tractors to pull in water from Lake Robertville to help tackle the fire in the High Fens. Photograph: Nicolas Lambert/Belga/Shutterstock Farmers have also been helping to battle the blaze, using their tractors to pull in water from Lake Robertville. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame? Read more Air support, provided by two water-bombing aircraft from Sweden and four helicopters – two from Belgium and two from the Netherlands – is crucial owing to the nature reserve’s complex and fragile terrain, which is made up of dense forest, peat bogs and raised wooden boardwalks where heavy firefighting vehicles risk sinking. Access to Lake Bütgenbach was prohibited on Sunday to allow the aircraft to refill. Authorities described the conditions as still challenging, although two fire fronts towards Jalhay and Monschau were now under control, said Belgium’s interior minister, Bernard Quintin, after visiting the crisis centre in Vottem on Sunday afternoon. “On this third day of fighting the fires, all resources remain mobilised on the ground,” he wrote on X, and he thanked all those involved. “We can also count on the solidarity of our European partners … Thank you to everyone who mobilised to fight the fires. United, we are stronger.” The fire, described by officials as the largest in Belgium’s modern history, began in an area that in 1911 was badly affected by massive wildfires during a drought. Map of Belgian wildfire Human-caused climate breakdown is supercharging extreme weather around the world, driving more frequent and deadlier disasters from heatwaves to floods to wildfires. Much of Europe is experiencing a new period of intense heat, creating conditions conducive to wildfire outbreaks. On Friday a fire engulfed ⁠homes in a Croatian holiday resort, killing one person, injuring 40 and forcing 1,200 to evacuate, officials said, as the EU warned that pockets of “very extreme” wildfire conditions stretched across the continent. Hundreds more people were evacuated from villages in western Germany and south-west France, while stranded holidaymakers were picked up from beaches threatened by flames in Greece and the army rescued historical relics in Spain. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Charles at Heathrow airport after being deported from Sweden. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Charles at Heathrow airport after being deported from Sweden. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Sweden ‘I have nothing in the UK at all’: British man torn from his Swedish wife and home Charles lands at Heathrow with just two bags and nowhere to go as a result of Brexit and Stockholm’s hardline immigration position Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.02 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 10.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Doubled over a Heathrow baggage trolley, the former British business director is sobbing uncontrollably, exhausted emotionally and physically after being deported from Sweden . Hours earlier the 65-year-old had been marched on to a plane in Stockholm, separated from his home and his Swedish wife after a five-year battle to stay in the country after Brexit came to an end. An only child with no children and no property in the UK, Charles has in effect been made homeless. He was last in the UK in 2022 for one week, and before that not since 2017 when he emigrated. Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since Brexit Read more “I have nothing, nothing in the UK at all,” says Charles as he shows a text from the British consulate explaining where in Heathrow those suddenly left homeless can get help. “All I want is to return to my wife, my home and my friends in Sweden and to live a quiet, peaceful life,” adds Charles, who does not want to publicly share his full identity. His forced flight on Tuesday shows that deportations of British citizens who lived in Sweden before Brexit are continuing. Stockholm has already deported 458 British people after rejected residency applications, a higher proportion in terms of its population than any EU member state. View image in fullscreen Charles is distraught after landing at Heathrow. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian The situation persists despite promises from opposition parties now on track to form a government that they will introduce urgent laws to give Britons a second chance to apply for residency. “I’ve done nothing wrong but feel I’ve been treated like a criminal,” Charles says. “Since arriving in Sweden nearly nine years ago, I’ve done everything I can to integrate myself into Swedish society. I’ve learned some basic Swedish, contributed to Swedish society and the Swedish economy, and for that, I’m being punished. Why are they doing this to good, honest, hard-working people like me and my wife?” Shortly after disembarking in London, he is sitting down in an airport cafe processing what has just happened. Pointing to a small holdall and a large reusable shopping bag, he says: “All I have is what my wife packed in my bag here with clothes and my little bag” – in which he has belongings handed back to him by the captain as he got off the plane. The bag includes a plastic envelope sealed and emblazoned with the words Kriminalvården, the Swedish Prison and Probation Service, containing meagre belongings. In it is a miniature tube of toothpaste, a toothbrush and earplugs given to him in the detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks. View image in fullscreen A bag containing a toothbrush, toothpaste and earplugs that was given to Charles in the Swedish detention centre where he was locked up for two weeks. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian A bright yellow envelope was also handed to him by the captain before disembarking, which he opens for the first time. Inside is a police document saying he does not need to be “escorted”. Another says he is being deported over a failed residency application under the Aliens Act – his latest legal attempt to stay in Sweden after a pre-Brexit residency application, made on time, was rejected. Charles’s plight started just over two weeks ago when he and his wife received a text requesting that they come to their local police station to discuss their migration case. They thought it was to discuss their five-year battle to persuade authorities they were in the country lawfully before Brexit. But he was immediately detained and told he would be deported. “It was an incredible shock. I was distraught. This is not about leaving Sweden, this is about me being forced to leave my wife and my house. They are separating me from my wife,” he said. “They said we think that if we don’t detain you, you will abscond from Sweden because you are not cooperating. “For the last nine years, all we’ve done is cooperate with them.” He said he begged authorities not to detain him, telling them he would go of his own accord but they said no. He asked if he could drive back to Britain “so at least I could take some belongings with me because I have nothing in the UK, and they said: ‘No, the decision has been made.’” View image in fullscreen A document envelope issued by the Swedish police authority. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Before Brexit, British citizens could live, work, study or retire in any other member state. Under EU law deportation was reserved for exceptional cases of criminality such as terrorism. After Brexit, Britons and EU citizens who had exercised those free movement rights were told their rights to remain in their host country would be guaranteed in the legally binding withdrawal agreement. The campaign group British in Europe has raised concerns about the hardline treatment in Sweden for years but this summer it became an election issue after a series of controversial cases emerged, including a removal order issued to a 78-year-old British widow, Joyce Thomas , who had been in the country for 21 years. View image in fullscreen Charles looking for help at Heathrow. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian A 74-year-old British man with dementia in full-time care was also ordered to leave after 25 years while another British man, 34, in the country since he was 10 years old, was deported in January . The cases raised questions about whether Sweden’s hardline immigration position had infected decision-making relating to Britons there before Brexit, a cohort with special protection. Charles says the experience has been humiliating, particularly as he spent a career in public service helping prisoners and unemployed people to start up businesses. “When I first moved to Sweden, I thought it was a wonderful place to live. Clean air. We were very close to the sea. Forests, nature, the people that I met when I first moved there were all generally very nice people. That did change,” he said. “Only two friends know what’s happened in the last couple of weeks. And they’re disgusted by it. One of them said, ‘I’m ashamed, I’m ashamed of what we’ve done to you’.” View image in fullscreen Charles leaves Heathrow airport, heading into an uncertain future. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Jane Golding , the chair of British in Europe, says “it is another case that raises the question of whether Swedish implementation is in line with the spirit of the withdrawal agreement,” referring to the legally binding treaty that Michel Barnier, then the EU’s chief negotiator on Britain’s exit from the EU, and Boris Johnson, the then prime minister, promised would protect EU citizens in the UK and British citizens in the EU. “This British man who has sufficient means and a home and a Swedish wife in Sweden now faces homelessness in the UK where he has nothing,” she says. “This wasn’t the intention of the EU and UK negotiators of the agreement who said that citizens should broadly be able to continue their lives as before,” she adds. She points out that, unlike the UK, there is no statutory body in any member state to oversee correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. “Monitoring and support resources for UK citizens in the EU trying to enforce their rights are not commensurate with those in the UK, where there is a dedicated independent monitoring authority. Unfunded volunteers trying to help are overwhelmed,” says Golding. https://bnn-news.com/interviews/bnn-inte.text: Streets in Cinevilla are adjustable to any requirement. · Photo: BNN Advertisements By Ilona Bērziņa Located in Slampe Parish, Tukums Municipality, Cinevilla is one of Latvia’s most unusual cultural and tourism attractions – the largest outdoor backlot in Northern Europe. Here, time periods, locations and entire cities change. Not digitally, but physically. Over the years, Cinevilla has recreated the atmosphere of early 20th-century Riga, complete with riverfront promenades, markets, boat piers and the wooden architecture of Pārdaugava. It has also hosted a 13th-century Semigallian settlement featuring a castle, harbor, ships and Viking-style buildings. The acclaimed historical drama Rūdolfa Mantojums, directed by Jānis Streičs, was filmed here as well. This year Cinevilla celebrates its 22nd anniversary. BNN spoke with its creator, film producer and director Andrejs Ēķis, about the unique story behind this extraordinary place. Cinevilla began as a set for a single film. Today it has become much more. How would you describe it? I won’t hide the fact that Cinevilla is my greatest hobby, passion and business – a place where I invest my heart, time and soul. Originally built for the historical feature film Defenders of Riga (Rīgas sargi), Cinevilla has evolved into one of Northern Europe’s most distinctive film production infrastructures. It is a ready-made cinematic world capable of transforming with remarkable speed into different countries, historical periods and realities. Advertisements Cinevilla is a functioning European backlot – a 150-hectare open-air production environment in Latvia where historical streets, river embankments, railway platforms, villages and architecture from various eras already exist and are simply waiting for cameras. One of our greatest strengths is the adaptability of our sets. The same street can become Riga, Vienna, Paris or New York simply by changing facades, signs and props. International producers seeking European-scale production opportunities without the overcrowded infrastructure of Prague, Budapest or Berlin highly value what Cinevilla offers – a world that is already built. For example, Blizzard of Souls (Dvēseļu putenis) used our railway station and platform, while the international series Sisi used a nineteenth-century European street and partially constructed building sets. In filmmaking, more than almost anywhere else, time is money, and Cinevilla is a tool that helps save time. Producers appreciate that Latvia still maintains the professional standard of a 12-hour filming day, whereas effective filming hours are increasingly restricted in many Western European countries. We also benefit from long summer daylight hours, allowing productions to shoot late into the evening without expensive artificial lighting. Another advantage is that we have our own hotel on-site, eliminating time-consuming travel between locations. If I had to describe Cinevilla in one sentence, I would say: “Cinevilla Studio is the Baltic backlot where Europe’s film industry can rapidly build the realities required for its stories.” After filming Defenders of Riga, it would have seemed logical to dismantle the sets. Why didn’t you? Advertisements I disagree that dismantling them would have been logical. We realized something very important: building a convincing historical city from scratch is extremely expensive. Once it exists, destroying it means eliminating a creative investment that can continue serving future productions. In much of Europe, film sets are part of a temporary economy. You spend enormous sums building them and then pay again to demolish them. At Cinevilla, the logic is completely different. Once you build a street, district or environment, it can remain useful for years. Imagine if long-running television series had to rebuild the same sets every season. Producers would go mad from the waste of time and money. That is why Cinevilla seeks not only feature films but also major international series and franchises—projects that live within these environments for years. There are excellent international examples. The Harry Potter films were shot at Leavesden Studios in the United Kingdom. Instead of destroying sets, costumes and props, they were preserved and reused. Warner Bros. later invested more than 100 million pounds into transforming the facility and opened the permanent Making of Harry Potter attraction in 2012. Another example is Game of Thrones in Northern Ireland, which became the foundation of an entire regional film industry. Many of its sets were preserved and transformed into the official Game of Thrones Studio Tour. Cinevilla sees itself moving in a similar direction—not as a static studio, but as a living cinematic environment. Advertisements Latvia offers film incentive programmes. Why are they attractive to foreign producers? Latvia operates a cash rebate system. A producer spends money in Latvia, submits reports and, if all requirements are met, receives a portion of those expenses back. Combined support can reach up to 50% of eligible local expenses—up to 30% from the national investment programme administered through LIAA and up to 20–25% through the Riga Film Fund. This allows Latvia to compete successfully with Lithuania, Estonia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Ireland and other countries offering production incentives. It is a win-win situation. Producers reduce production costs, while Latvia gains jobs for local crews, equipment rental companies, hotels, catering providers, transport services, security companies and production infrastructure. I am pleased that policymakers increasingly understand that exporting film and television production services can generate substantial long-term economic benefits. How has the streaming era changed the industry? Advertisements Streaming has fundamentally transformed European filmmaking. Previously there was a clear release sequence: cinema release, pay television, DVD sales and finally free television. Streaming has made the process far more flexible. Films can now appear in cinemas and on streaming platforms almost simultaneously. A recent European Audiovisual Observatory study found that films performing well in cinemas receive, on average, eleven times more viewing time on streaming platforms than films with weak theatrical releases. This creates opportunities for smaller film-producing countries. EU regulations require streaming services to ensure that at least 30% of their catalogues consist of European works and that those works receive visibility. Of course, visibility does not guarantee success among thousands of available titles. Nevertheless, theatrical premieres remain important cultural events, particularly for major franchises supported by sequels, spin-offs, fan communities, merchandise and global marketing campaigns. What does the streaming boom mean for film studios? Advertisements This is exactly the right moment for studios like Cinevilla. Streaming platforms demand facilities capable of supporting entire seasons of television productions, not merely a few days of shooting. Competitive studios therefore need flexible sets, outdoor environments, interior spaces, workshops, costumes, props, technical equipment, virtual production capabilities and experienced local crews. Cinevilla provides all of this in one place. Our ability to adapt quickly to changing industry requirements is one of the keys to our success. That is why I always say that Cinevilla is a living studio. Its artificial worlds can rapidly transform into settings for fantasy films, westerns, thrillers, historical dramas, romantic productions or television series. Cinevilla is essentially a backlot film city. Many facades exist only on one side, buildings may be shallow and windows may not be real, but on camera everything appears entirely convincing. That is the magic of cinema. You often say: “Differentiate or die.” What makes Cinevilla different? Advertisements We have 150 hectares of land that can be transformed according to the most ambitious and unconventional creative demands. We can dig trenches, create artificial rivers, reshape gravel pits, transport sand and timber, build fortifications and stage controlled explosions. Unlike many European locations surrounded by dense urban environments, we are not constrained by endless approval procedures. Things happen faster and more efficiently here. Nearby farms and rural infrastructure also make it easy to work with horses, livestock and other elements often required for historical productions. Perhaps the most interesting thing about Cinevilla is that it no longer belongs solely to the film industry. When productions are not taking place, the site hosts festivals, corporate events, concerts, obstacle races and private celebrations. Events such as Stipro Skrējiens and Danger Fest have transformed the streets into alternative realities filled with lights, performances and actors. That gives the place a unique energy. If you had to compare Cinevilla with Hollywood, what would you say? In many ways, Cinevilla does what Hollywood did during its earliest years in the beginning of the twentieth century. We are building a place where cinematic reality can become any story imaginable. Hollywood is a global dream factory. Cinevilla is smaller, more modest and rougher around the edges. But the mechanism of cinematic magic is exactly the same. Using timber, plasterboard, paint, lighting, digital post-production and imagination, we create realities that audiences are willing to believe.
